theme: I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 116. This is a song of thanks from someone who was near death and was saved. It is part of the Hallel, sung at Passover. Read it aloud as a personal testimony.
settingTheScene: Psalm 116 is a thanksgiving psalm. The singer has cried out in deep trouble and God has answered, and now he comes to the congregation to keep his vows. The psalm is anonymous, but it is easy to imagine David or Hezekiah behind it. Because it belongs to the Hallel, Jesus and his disciples almost certainly sang it on the night before he died, a few hours before Gethsemane.
observation: “I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice and my pleas for mercy” (v. 1).
“Because he inclined his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live” (v. 2).
“The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me; I suffered distress and anguish” (v. 3).
“Gracious is the LORD, and righteous; our God is merciful” (v. 5).
“The LORD preserves the simple; when I was brought low, he saved me” (v. 6).
“For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling” (v. 8).
“What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits to me?” (v. 12).
“Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (v. 15).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with love: “I love the LORD.” The reason is not a general feeling but a specific answer. He heard my voice. The God of the universe bent down his ear to a person in need. The psalmist concludes that he will call on God for as long as he lives.

Then he tells his story. Death had wrapped around him like a snare. Distress and anguish found him. In that darkness he called, “O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul!” and the LORD answered. The character of the God who answers is given in verse 5: gracious, righteous, and merciful. These three words belong together. His grace is never at odds with his justice.

He says he was “brought low,” and the LORD saved him. Now he can rest: “Return, O my soul, to your rest, for the LORD has dealt bountifully with you.” Deliverance from death, tears, and stumbling is the work of God alone.

Then comes one of the great questions of the Psalter: “What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits to me?” The answer is not a payment, since no one can repay God. It is worship and trust: “I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD.” He will pay his vows in the presence of all the people.

Verse 15 is for the grieving: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.” Death is not meaningless to God. Every believer who dies is watched over with care.

Read this psalm beside the Last Supper. Jesus lifted a cup that night, and the psalm was in his mouth. He would soon drink a cup of suffering so that we might receive the cup of salvation. The cry of the psalmist became the cry of Jesus, and the deliverance he sang about was won in his death and resurrection.
connection: Psalm 18:4-6 describes similar cords of death. Matthew 26:30 and Mark 14:26 say they sang a hymn before going out. Luke 22:17-20 describes the cup at the Supper. 1 Corinthians 10:16 speaks of the cup of blessing. Romans 12:1 offers the answer to “What shall I render?” Hebrews 2:14-15 says Christ delivered those enslaved by fear of death. Revelation 14:13 speaks of those who die in the Lord.
application:
Tell the story of a time God answered you. Write it down or tell it to someone.

Answer verse 12 for yourself. What will you render to the LORD this week? Make it concrete.

If you have lost a believer, rest in verse 15. Their death is precious to the LORD.
prayerPrompts: Tell God that you love him and why.
Thank him for delivering you from death and tears.
Ask him what you can render to him for all his benefits.
